hero.subtitle: Whether you were injured at a lodge, ski resort, restaurant, or job site along Big Bear Boulevard, a work injury can leave you with medical bills and lost wages fast. We can review both your workers' comp options and any third-party claim to help you understand your rights and next steps.

about.title: Big Bear Lake Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Big Bear Lake's economy runs on tourism, hospitality, and outdoor recreation, and that means workers face a wide range of on-the-job risks — from lifting injuries in hotel kitchens and ski shops to falls on icy walkways near Moonridge Road or equipment accidents at maintenance and construction sites. Most workplace injuries here get handled through California workers' compensation, which generally pays medical care and partial wage replacement regardless of who was at fault. But when a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, or another driver contributed to your injury, a separate claim against that third party may also be available. Sorting out which path applies, and whether both apply, is not something you should have to figure out alone while recovering. We handle workplace injury claims for Big Bear Lake workers and can review the details of what happened and explain your realistic options, without pressure or upfront cost.
commonInjuries: Slip-and-fall injuries on stairs, decks, or icy walkways
Lifting and repetitive strain injuries in hospitality jobs
Ladder and fall injuries at maintenance or construction sites
Vehicle collisions while driving for work duties
Burns or cuts from kitchen and food-service equipment

whyChoose.title: Why You Should Review Your Options With an Attorney

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Picture
items.desc: California workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but if a third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker contributed to your injury, a separate claim may be possible alongside it.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a work injury to your employer, and missing that window can complicate your claim — we can help you understand what documentation you need and when.

items.title: Retaliation Is Illegal
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from punishing workers for reporting an injury or filing a claim, and we can advise you on your rights if you're worried about your job.

items.question: I was hurt working at a resort near Moonridge Road — do I file workers' comp or a lawsuit?
items.answer: In most cases, workers' comp is your primary route against your employer regardless of fault. But if another company, like a maintenance contractor or equipment supplier, played a role in the accident, you may also have a separate third-party claim. We can look at the specifics and explain which options apply to your situation.

items.question: What if my employer says I waited too long to report my injury?
items.answer: California generally requires injuries to be reported to your employer within 30 days, so timing does matter. Even if you're past that window, it's worth speaking with us, since there can be exceptions and other options depending on the facts.

items.question: Can I get fired for filing a workers' comp claim in Big Bear Lake?
items.answer: No — California law prohibits retaliation against employees for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim. If you believe you've faced retaliation, we can advise you on next steps and how your rights may be protected.
